sittings.bodyEn: From this point the aim is to charge as much as the value will support, including amounts that feel extreme. Large companies already charge heavily for things that cost them very little, such as adding a phone user, making a pill, or selling attention. Stay under what the product is worth to the buyer, and charge far more than it costs you to deliver, even many times more, while the buyer still feels they received a bargain. A photography company he is involved with moved the average ticket from $300 to $1,500, a fivefold rise, while spending less time per customer and raising satisfaction. Weekly profit moved from about $1,000 to about $38,000, which funded more locations, better jobs, and about $500,000 to children's charities. They found what clients valued most, did more of that, and cut the rest.

terms.hook: Charge far more than delivery costs, and still less than the value the buyer receives.

sittings.bodyEn: The value equation is his name for four drivers that set what an offer is worth. On the top, increase the dream outcome and the perceived likelihood of achievement. On the bottom, decrease the time delay and the effort and sacrifice. His father's questions were the same four: what will I make, how will I know it will happen, how long will it take, and what is expected of me. The picture multiplies the two top drivers, multiplies the two bottom drivers, and then divides. A short free walkthrough sits with the chapter, and these four drivers are the part to learn first.

terms.hook: Dream outcome times likelihood, divided by time delay times effort and sacrifice.
The result they already want, which you try to increase.
How sure they feel that the result will happen for them.

sittings.bodyEn: Early in his career he pushed the top of the equation with bigger promises and more proof. Anyone can make a larger claim, so that move is common and less distinctive. The harder contest is time delay and effort, and the strongest companies make the result feel immediate and nearly effortless. A simpler phone made other phones feel clumsy, a one-click store made buying feel instant, and a streaming shelf made television feel effortless. He writes the equation as division so a bottom near zero pushes value toward infinity, even when the dream on top is modest. The picture of that limit is a purchase that instantly creates a lean midsection, or a signed agreement that makes the phone start ringing with ready buyers.

terms.hook: Time delay and effort, the pair to drive toward zero.

sittings.bodyEn: Buyers pay for the improvement they can actually perceive. The offer becomes valuable when they perceive better odds, a shorter wait, and an easier path. In the London underground, rider satisfaction jumped more from a dotted map of the next train than from actually faster trains. The map cost a fraction of what speed would cost, and it reduced the felt wait and the boredom of standing on the platform. Logical fixes are usually already tried, so he hunts psychological ones: mirrors in an elevator so people forget the ride, hosts people enjoy so they wish the trip were longer, or fewer units at a higher price so desire rises. State the four drivers clearly, or the market never counts them in the price.

terms.hook: Buyers pay for the change they can feel, including a shorter wait they can see.
A fix for how the wait or the effort feels, after the obvious logical fix has already been tried.

sittings.bodyEn: The dream outcome is the future they already picture, and the job is to channel that desire through something they can buy. Common desires are to be seen as beautiful, respected, powerful, loved, or higher in status. Makeup, creams, pills, shapewear, surgery, and training can all carry the same wish to look beautiful, and under that wish is often status inside a group. Between two different dreams, people usually pay more for the one that lifts status, which is why many men will pay more to make money than to look better. Someone who rejected a flashy sports car still preferred a minivan, because among parent friends the minivan raised her standing and the sports car would lower it. When you write the benefit, add how other people will see the win, such as friends watching a drive sail past theirs.

terms.hook: How the buyer believes others will rank them after the result.
Use a want that already exists, and attach your offer to it.

sittings.bodyEn: Perceived likelihood of achievement was the last driver he added, because the other three felt incomplete. People pay more to be a surgeon's ten-thousandth patient than the first, and some would want to be paid to go first. The operation can be the same work, and the veteran may finish faster while charging more. What changed is the buyer's belief that they will actually get the result. You raise that belief with the message, the proof, what you include or leave out, and the guarantee. When two offers promise the same dream, this driver plus time and effort set the price, which is how one path can be worth $50,000 and another $5.

terms.hook: Their belief that this purchase will work for them, which proof and guarantees can raise.

sittings.bodyEn: Time delay is the gap between the payment and the promised benefit. People buy the long-term dream, and they stay because of short wins along the way. A gym owner might be buying about $239,000 a year, which takes months, so an early win is ads running and a first $2,000 sale inside seven days. A physique goal might take a year, while energy, desire, and new friends show up sooner, and a harder early diet plus a quick introduction creates a win that keeps them enrolled. People who taste an early victory are more likely to continue than people who wait for the final result. A year of waiting looks expensive beside an afternoon procedure, which is one reason people pay about $25,000 for liposuction and a tuck while hesitating at $100 a month for a bootcamp.

terms.hook: How long they believe they must wait between paying and feeling the result.
A small, early result that proves they are on the path and keeps them going.

sittings.bodyEn: Speed is what people pay for when a free version already exists. People pay for speed even when a slower version costs them nothing. A private motor-vehicle desk can charge about $50 to skip a long public line. An overnight courier beats cheap mail when the package has to arrive the next day. Paid music beat slow free music by starting instantly, and a hired ride beats walking for the same reason. When the rival is free, put the weight of the offer on speed.

terms.hook: People pay for a quicker version of something they could otherwise get for nothing.

sittings.bodyEn: Effort and sacrifice are the extra costs along the way, both bills and feelings. A fitness path, in his side-by-side, can mean waking one or two hours earlier, losing five to ten hours a week, dropping favorite foods, hunger, soreness, embarrassment, injury risk, nausea, meal prep, costlier groceries, new clothes, and the fear of gaining the weight back. The surgical path in the same comparison is falling asleep, waking up lean, and being sore for two to four weeks. Surgeons advertise against the gym hours and the diets that fail. Done-for-you costs more than do-it-yourself because the buyer spends less effort and also believes an expert raises the odds. The dream can be identical, and the two vehicles still deserve very different prices.

terms.hook: Everything else the buyer must give up or endure on the way to the result.
You carry the effort, so the price can be higher than a do-it-yourself version of the same dream.

sittings.bodyEn: He scores each driver as present or thin and adds them, so two vehicles with the same dream can be compared. A daily meditation practice and a calming pill can both promise ease, lower anxiety, and a sense of well-being. The practice scores low on belief, because people doubt they will sit every day, partial on time, and empty on effort, for a total around one and a half out of four. The pill scores full on belief, about fifteen minutes until it is felt, and the effort of swallowing, for four out of four. That gap is why the pill category became an enormous business while almost no meditation company reached that scale, even when the practice is the healthier choice. Supplements, a market around $123 billion, are roughly twice the health-club market around $62 billion, because a shake is faster and easier than a daily gym visit, and people more readily pay $200 for pills than $29 a month to train.

terms.hook: Identical results can have very different value once speed, effort, and belief change.

sittings.bodyEn: You can spend your energy arguing that people ought to choose the harder, healthier path. You can also sell what they already value, and use that sale to deliver what they actually need. He takes the second route and calls it a win on both sides. You make the change you care about, and the business keeps a profit. The useful skill is knowing the difference between what people value and what is good for them. The four drivers are the design tools for that trade.

terms.hook: Sell the result people already want, and use it to deliver the result they need.

sittings.bodyEn: The value equation raises two drivers and shrinks two others. Bigger claims sit on the top and are the easier move. The companies he points to spend their effort on the bottom. Choose the pair this chapter tells you to push down.
sittings.prompt: Which two drivers does the value equation tell you to push down?
choices: Time delay, and effort and sacrifice
Dream outcome, and the odds they believe they will succeed
Ad spend, and the number of impressions
Guarantee length, and the number of bonuses
